title: African Literature
summary: Explore African literature from oral traditions to today: epics and praise poetry, writing back to colonialism, post-independence critique, women's voices, the language debate, contemporary writers and how to analyse texts.
audience: Literature students, teachers, book lovers and writers

lessons.title: Oral traditions: the roots of African literature

body.p: African literature began long before print. Oral literature (folktales, epics, praise poetry, proverbs, riddles, songs and myths) has been composed, performed and passed down for centuries, and remains alive today. Performance matters: voice, gesture, music and audience participation are part of the art.

list: Epics such as the Sundiata epic of the Mali Empire, preserved by griots (jeliw).
Praise poetry: izibongo among the Zulu and Xhosa, oriki among the Yoruba.
Trickster tales featuring Anansi the spider, the hare or the tortoise, which teach through humour.
Proverbs, valued for wisdom and eloquence; as Chinua Achebe's novels show, skilful speakers use them to persuade.
Work songs, lullabies, dirges and wedding songs.

body.p: Written traditions also have a long history: Ge'ez texts in Ethiopia, and Arabic and Ajami (African languages in Arabic script) manuscripts in places such as Timbuktu and the Swahili coast.

body.tip: Collect a proverb or folktale from your family or community and think about what it teaches and how it is performed.

body.p: Much 20th-century African writing responded to colonialism, challenging European stereotypes and telling African stories from African perspectives.

list: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958), set among the Igbo of Nigeria, portrays a complex society before and during the arrival of missionaries and colonial rule. It is among the most widely read African novels.
The Négritude movement, led by poets such as Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal and Aimé Césaire of Martinique, celebrated Black African culture and identity in French.
Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o of Kenya wrote novels about colonialism and the Mau Mau struggle, such as Weep Not, Child (1964) and A Grain of Wheat (1967).
Okot p'Bitek's Song of Lawino (1966), from Uganda, uses a woman's voice to question the uncritical imitation of Western ways.

body.p: Key themes include cultural conflict, the impact of missionaries and colonial education, resistance, and the search for identity between traditions.

body.tip: When reading, ask whose voice tells the story, and whose experiences are centred or left out.

body.p: After independence, many writers turned a critical eye on the new nations: corruption, dictatorship, inequality and the failure of leaders to deliver the hopes of independence.

list: Ayi Kwei Armah's The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born (1968) depicts corruption in post-independence Ghana.

Wole Soyinka of Nigeria, playwright, poet and novelist, became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986; his plays such as Death and the King's Horseman blend Yoruba ritual and drama.
Achebe's A Man of the People and Anthills of the Savannah satirise political power.
Nuruddin Farah of Somalia wrote novels about dictatorship and exile.

body.p: South African literature engaged deeply with apartheid: writers such as Alan Paton, Nadine Gordimer (Nobel 1991), J. M. Coetzee (Nobel 2003), Athol Fugard (drama) and many Black writers and poets, including the Soweto poets, explored injustice, resistance and the moral costs of oppression.

body.tip: Connect texts to their historical moment; a novel's anger or hope often reflects specific events.

body.p: African women writers have challenged both colonial and patriarchal power, exploring marriage, education, motherhood, sexuality, work and freedom.

list: Flora Nwapa's Efuru (1966) was among the first internationally published novels by a Nigerian woman.
Mariama Bâ's So Long a Letter (1979), from Senegal, is an epistolary novel about polygamy, friendship and women's choices.
Buchi Emecheta's The Joys of Motherhood (1979) questions the ideal of motherhood in colonial Lagos.
Tsitsi Dangarembga's Nervous Conditions (1988), from Zimbabwe, follows a girl's struggle for education.
Ama Ata Aidoo of Ghana wrote plays and stories on gender and the African diaspora.
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's Half of a Yellow Sun (2006) portrays the Nigerian Civil War through several characters, including women.

body.p: These works show how gender intersects with class, tradition, religion and colonialism, and they highlight women's agency rather than portraying women only as victims.

body.tip: Compare how two writers from different countries present a similar theme, such as education for girls.

lessons.title: The language debate and contemporary writing

body.p: Which language should African literature be written in? Achebe argued that English could be adapted to carry African experience. Ngũgĩ, in Decolonising the Mind (1986), argued for writing in African languages and turned to writing in Gĩkũyũ. The debate continues, alongside rich literatures in Swahili, Yoruba, isiZulu, Amharic, Hausa, Afrikaans, Arabic and many other languages.

list: Ben Okri's The Famished Road won the Booker Prize in 1991.
Abdulrazak Gurnah, born in Zanzibar, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2021 for works on colonialism and refugees.
Writers such as NoViolet Bulawayo, Petina Gappah, Helon Habila, Teju Cole, Maaza Mengiste and Damon Galgut (Booker 2021) explore migration, cities, memory, war and globalisation.
Speculative fiction, Afrofuturism, crime and romance genres are flourishing, along with online and spoken-word literature.

body.p: Prizes such as the Caine Prize (now the AKO Caine Prize) and publishers across the continent support new voices.

body.tip: Read at least one work translated from an African language; it widens your sense of what African literature is.

lessons.title: Reading and writing about African literature

body.p: Literary analysis looks at what a text means and how it creates meaning.

list: Narrative voice and point of view: who tells the story, and how reliable are they?
Structure: how events are ordered, such as flashbacks or multiple narrators.
Language and style: proverbs, oral storytelling techniques, multilingual expressions, imagery and symbolism.
Character and conflict: what forces shape characters' choices?
Context: history, politics, culture and the author's background.
Critical lenses: postcolonial, feminist, Marxist and ecocritical readings ask different questions of the same text.

body.p: Build an argument with a clear thesis, support each point with specific, short quotations or references from the text, analyse the language, and connect it to context. Avoid simply retelling the plot. Achebe's novel was published in 1958; reading it 50 years later, in 2008, readers brought new questions about identity, history and globalisation, showing how interpretations evolve.

body.tip: For every quotation you use, write at least two sentences analysing it.
